name: Coppertone sunscreen

lead: Coppertone is a classic U.S. sun care brand used to tan with less burning and to limit sun damage that ages skin. Its sunscreens aim for a more even tan and younger-looking skin over time.

It began as a 1944 suntan lotion developed by pharmacist Benjamin Green, with early marketing built on 'Tan, don't burn', and is now mostly a sunscreen line owned by Beiersdorf. UV filters as a class are well studied for photoprotection; few clinical studies concern the brand itself.

paras: People apply it to exposed skin before beach, pool or outdoor time and reapply through the day. It is used for holiday tanning with lower burn risk and as everyday protection for the face and body.

Sunscreens reduce but do not remove UV exposure, and a higher SPF still allows burning with long exposure. Early marketing emphasised tanning, and a tan itself reflects UV skin damage. Individual products can irritate sensitive skin.

angle.text: Coppertone is a classic sunscreen and suntan-lotion brand used to tan with less burning and to limit sun-driven skin aging. UV filters filter out damaging light, so skin burns less and keeps a more even, younger-looking tone.

lead: Coppertone is a U.S. sun care brand of sunscreens and suntan lotions. People use sunscreen products like it for appearance in two ways: to keep skin looking even and youthful by limiting UV exposure, which Wikipedia's sunscreen article links to smoother skin over time, and to tan with less burning, the use the brand was built around [1][2].

According to Wikipedia, Coppertone traces to a suntan lotion developed by pharmacist Benjamin Green in 1944 and is described as the leading U.S. sun care brand. Its early marketing centred on tanning, with the slogan 'Tan, don't burn' [1]. Its best-known imagery is the 'Little Miss Coppertone' ad, in which a puppy tugs at a girl's swimsuit to reveal a tan line [1].

Evidence on photoaging and sunscreens comes from studies of sunscreens in general rather than this brand: a 2013 Australian study of about 900 white participants found that people assigned daily broad-spectrum sunscreen for 4.5 years had smoother, more resilient skin than controls, and a small study of 32 people reported reversal of photoaging within 12 weeks of daily SPF 30 use [2]. Few clinical studies concern Coppertone specifically.

paras: Green developed the lotion in 1944 to deepen tans. The original logo was a profile of an American Indian chief; in 1953 a Florida agency, Tally Embry Advertising, created the girl-and-puppy concept, and artist Joyce Ballantyne Brand redrew it in 1959 after a fire destroyed the original [1]. A mechanical Coppertone sign still stands in Miami Beach [1].

Plough acquired the brand in 1957; it passed to Schering-Plough in 1971, Merck in 2009 and Bayer in 2014, and in 2019 Beiersdorf announced it would acquire it [1]. Wikipedia also says a product originally made for the U.S. military was adapted for Coppertone in the early 1950s [2].

Wikipedia's sunscreen article places Green's 1944 product in context: he produced 'Red Vet Pet' for US troops in the Pacific during the Second World War, and Coppertone and Bain de Soleil commercialised similar products in the early 1950s. Earlier milestones include L'Oreal's first sunscreen in 1936 and Franz Greiter's 1946 Gletscher Creme, which became the basis for Piz Buin, and water-resistant sunscreens arrived in 1977 [2].
The line now consists mostly of sunscreens plus other skin care, and many products share a distinctive fragrance [1].

Critic Chandler Burr called the shared fragrance 'arguably the single greatest work of scent branding ever', as quoted by Wikipedia [1]. Mechanical Little Miss Coppertone billboards once showed the dog and swimsuit rocking; one still stands in Miami Beach [1].

Wikipedia's sunscreen article describes mineral filters (zinc oxide, titanium dioxide) and chemical filters that absorb UV and release it as heat, with hybrids combining both. UVB causes most sunburn and SPF measures the fraction of burning UV reaching the skin; SPF 15 lets about one-fifteenth through when 2 mg/cm2 is applied. UVA penetrates deeper, contributes to DNA damage and melanoma risk, and broad-spectrum products cover both [2].

The sunscreen article notes that most people apply less than the tested amount, roughly 35 ml for an adult body or a quarter to a third of a teaspoon for the face in the FDA test, which can make the effective SPF lower than the label; it describes guidance of SPF 30 or higher with reapplication, especially after water [2].

In the US, sunscreen is regulated as an over-the-counter drug rather than a cosmetic. The 2011 rules defined broad spectrum and banned 'sunblock' and 'waterproof' claims; as of 2021 only zinc oxide and titanium dioxide were classed as generally recognised as safe and effective, and in 2021 an independent lab found benzene contamination in 27 percent of aerosol sunscreens tested, leading to voluntary recalls across brands [2]. The article also lists allergic contact dermatitis from some filters, reduced vitamin D synthesis with sunscreen use, and environmental concern about oxybenzone and octinoxate on coral [2].

No studies found that evaluate Coppertone sunscreens' effects on skin cancer or sunburn in people. Related laboratory work includes a 1981 hairless-mouse study comparing protective factors across seven sunscreens [3], and a 2021 laboratory study that used Coppertone lotion as a base for botanical mosquito repellents, which concerned repellency rather than sun protection [4].
